[[speaker:rhen]]“He needed someone who would remain if the answer was difficult.”

Her eyes lowered.

[[speaker:rhen]]“Comfort is not certainty. Do not make a promise the patient must later survive losing.”

Each correction landed differently.

Some flushed. Some argued. Han wrote everything down.

Sera listened from the doorway.

Rhen did not teach like a sect master. He offered no mystery and demanded no reverence. He made knowledge plain enough to challenge.

That made it harder to hide behind obedience.

In the afternoon, he laid twelve bundles before them. Each held the same herbs in slightly different condition.

[[speaker:rhen]]“Prepare fever medicine.”

Only Minseok refused.

[[speaker:minseok]]“Three bundles contain moon-vine harvested after flowering. It will lower heat and damage the lungs.”

Seo checked and found he was right.

Chen looked offended by the plant.

[[speaker:chen]]“Why place the wrong herb there?”

[[speaker:sera]]“Because wrong herbs do not announce themselves in actual clinics.”

They spent two hours salvaging what remained safe. Six useful doses emerged from twelve apparently complete bundles. Rhen made them record the rejected material and the reason for every decision.

By dusk, the apprentices had learned four kinds of failure and produced medicine for six patients. None of it felt heroic.

Then a courier collapsed outside.

His breathing had stopped.

Training vanished from every face.

Rhen knelt. Two fingers touched the courier's chest. A warmth like spring sunlight passed once through the man's body.

His heart moved.

His lungs followed.

No flourish. No announced technique. Only life returning so naturally that the twelve stood frozen around it.

The courier coughed.

Rhen looked up.

[[speaker:rhen]]“Han, airway. Yeo, pulse. Bai, find his route and ask what he carried. Seo, smell his sleeve.”

They moved.

The miracle lasted one heartbeat.

The work continued for three hours.

They discovered heat exhaustion, an untreated rib injury and stimulant powder taken to complete one impossible route. Bai traced the delivery to a merchant who had threatened to withhold the courier's wages. Jiang wrote the name down beside the treatment cost. Sera quietly copied it into another ledger.

Afterward Chen found Rhen washing blood from his hands.

[[speaker:chen]]“If you can do that, why teach us bandages?”

Rhen dried his hands.

[[speaker:rhen]]“Because I was here.”

He nodded toward the dark road beyond the door.

[[speaker:rhen]]“Most people who need help are somewhere I am not.”

For the first time, Chen had no answer.

The dead branch remained on the classroom shelf for the rest of the year.

title: The First Night Shift
text:
The first night shift began with a broken axle and became a flood of human problems.

A passenger cart overturned outside town during hard rain. Villagers carried the injured into Second Spring in doors, blankets and one grain basket emptied for the purpose.

Twelve people arrived at once: three with fractures, two with internal injuries, four children in shock, an elderly woman who could not remember her own name, and a driver insisting he was unhurt while blood filled one boot.

Then the kitchen chimney caught fire.

Sera stared at the smoke.

[[speaker:sera]]“Of course it did.”

Tang had already found the buckets.

Han divided the courtyard before anyone appointed her. Severe injuries nearest Rhen. Walking wounded along the eastern wall. Families under the awning where Mei could keep them informed.

She placed the driver near the centre despite his protest.

[[speaker:mira]]“If the boot is filling, you are not unhurt.”

[[speaker:customer]]“I can still stand.”

[[speaker:mira]]“Then stand here.”

Yeo anchored the driver's failing pulse. Seo identified the sweet scent of a pain-numbing powder that had hidden his symptoms. Gu held a fractured cart beam while Ren cut it into splints. Bai built a message chain between treatment room, courtyard and village shrine.

Chen tried to be everywhere.

He carried needles to Rhen, abandoned them to fetch water, crossed back when one child screamed and nearly collided with Bai carrying a list of patient names.

Sera caught his collar as he crossed the room for the fourth time.

[[speaker:sera]]“Choose one patient.”

[[speaker:chen]]“They all need—”

[[speaker:sera]]“Then trust someone else with the rest.”

He looked around as though noticing the other eleven for the first time.

Sera pointed toward the driver.

[[speaker:sera]]“Yeo cannot hold that circulation forever.”

Chen knelt beside him and stayed.

Lin found wheel grease on the driver's cuff and realized the axle had been cut rather than broken. Jiang wrote the detail down but did not let the discovery interrupt treatment. Minseok rejected two bundles of old clotting moss and ran through rain to the farm for fresh leaves.

The chimney smoke thickened.

Tang sent Ren to close the kitchen vent, Gu to pull the burning shelf away from the wall and one of the uninjured passengers to form a bucket line. She never left the treatment area. Sera saw the solution organize itself and returned to the patients without taking command back.

The elderly woman's breathing worsened.

Rhen was repairing a child's torn meridian pathway. He could have crossed the room and solved both cases. Instead, his voice remained calm.

[[speaker:rhen]]“Han?”

Han checked the woman's neck, pupils and fingertips. A dark swelling hid beneath wet silver hair.

[[speaker:mira]]“Not memory loss. Pressure inside the skull.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“What do you need?”

[[speaker:mira]]“Yeo. Clean needles. Quiet.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“Yeo is occupied.”

Han looked toward the driver. Chen had taken the lower pulse but not yet stabilized it.

[[speaker:mira]]“Then I need Chen to succeed.”

The whole room seemed to narrow around that answer.

Chen adjusted his hands. Yeo corrected the angle once, then released the circulation into Chen's care.

The driver's pulse faltered.

Chen did not chase it with force. He followed the rhythm Rhen had taught, supporting the return rather than demanding it.

The pulse steadied.

Yeo crossed to Han.

Gu cleared the area. Bai redirected questions. Mei sat with the woman's frightened granddaughter and explained each action without promising the outcome.

Han placed the first needle.

Rain hammered the awning. The kitchen shelf collapsed with a crash. Nobody in the treatment circle turned toward it.

Sera watched the room become more than twelve separate efforts.

It was ugly. Messages were repeated. Two bowls shattered. Chen used the wrong knot and swore loudly enough for three children to learn a new word. Ren's first splint failed. Mei cried in the pantry for thirty seconds after telling a mother that her son might lose movement in one hand.

Sera found her there washing her face with both hands.

[[speaker:mei]]“I did not promise.”

[[speaker:sera]]“No.”

[[speaker:mei]]“It still hurt her.”

[[speaker:sera]]“Yes.”

Mei waited for something that would make the answer easier.

Sera handed her a clean cloth.

[[speaker:sera]]“Go back anyway.”

Mei did.

Near midnight, one child stopped feeling two fingers. Ren rebuilt the splint while Rhen guided the torn meridian around swelling. The boy's mother stood close enough to obstruct everyone until Gu gave her a task: count each breath aloud. Her voice shook, but the counting kept the child calm and allowed Yeo to hear when his breathing changed.

The sabotaged axle remained a question for later. Lin sealed the cut pin in cloth and placed it in Sera's ledger drawer. He did not pursue whoever might have done it while injured people still needed care.

That choice mattered to her.

Before dawn, the elderly woman spoke her granddaughter's name. The driver kept his leg. The child with the meridian injury moved all five fingers, though the smallest two remained weak.

Every patient was alive.

The chimney fire had destroyed one pot and blackened half the kitchen. Sera regarded that as a secondary victory.

The apprentices collapsed wherever there was floor.

Rhen covered them with spare blankets. Sera stepped over Chen, who had fallen asleep holding a roll of bandage like a weapon.

[[speaker:sera]]“They are terrible.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“Less terrible than yesterday.”

[[speaker:sera]]“One of them set the kitchen on fire.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“The chimney.”

[[speaker:sera]]“The chimney had assistance.”

Mei murmured in her sleep. Han's hand remained around the elderly woman's wrist, counting a pulse even while unconscious.

Sera crouched and gently moved the hand onto a folded cloth.

She returned to find Rhen watching her.

[[speaker:sera]]“What?”

[[speaker:rhen]]“Nothing.”

[[speaker:sera]]“That expression is not nothing.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“You moved her hand.”

[[speaker:sera]]“It was uncomfortable.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“For Han?”

[[speaker:sera]]“For me to look at.”

He wisely stopped smiling.

When the twelve woke, breakfast waited on the tables. None remembered preparing it.

Rhen reviewed the night only after everyone had eaten. He named what had worked, what had failed and which lucky outcomes must not be mistaken for correct decisions. Han's organization had saved time. Chen had finally trusted Yeo. Tang had contained a fire without abandoning medicine. Lin had preserved evidence without letting curiosity outrank patients.

Then he made them clean the entire tea house.

They began calling Rhen Teacher that morning.

By evening, three had accidentally called Sera Mother.

She threatened to double their training.

Nobody believed she wanted them to stop.

title: A Bell at the Door
text:
The water problem returned when the first true heat of summer reached Lanyun.

The shallow cistern dried. The old well gave up mud. Rhen's rare medicinal beds began curling at their edges despite careful rationing.

Sera caught him carrying washing water toward the frostroot.

[[speaker:sera]]“Put that down.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“The roots are stressed.”

[[speaker:sera]]“So are the apprentices.”

Upstairs, twelve people had discovered that sharing two wash basins in summer produced less fellowship than expected. Chen had begun bathing before dawn to avoid the queue. Seo responded by waking earlier. Gu slept beside one basin twice before Sera prohibited territorial claims over household water.

Rhen returned the bucket.

They reduced tea service to four blends and stopped washing the front stones. The fisherman complained that the dust changed the establishment's character. Sera handed him a broom.

He decided the character was acceptable.

The farm could not be treated so easily. Common bitterbark tolerated dry soil, but moon-vine weakened within hours and frostroot required steady moisture beneath the surface. Losing either would erase months of work and medicine promised to Physician Su.

They hired a well digger, who struck granite and declared the underground stone impossible. A geomancer charged three silver to announce that the water dragon had moved elsewhere.

Lin followed him afterward and discovered he had made the same diagnosis at four dry farms.

Sera recovered two of the three silver. The geomancer kept one in exchange for leaving Lanyun before she explained the alternative.

Rhen continued marking the buried stream with blue string, but the line vanished beneath the rear wall and divided around a shelf of granite. Breaking the wrong section could drown the cellar or collapse the kitchen.

For once, overwhelming strength was not the useful answer.

[[speaker:chen]]“Could Teacher not cut through the stone?”

[[speaker:dabin]]“He could also remove the entire courtyard. That would technically reach the water.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“An excellent example of why ability is not a plan.”

Sera sent them both to carry water from the public well.

At dusk, a bell rang at the front door.

Not the hanging shop bell. This sound came from metal striking stone—small, low and irregular. The first note barely reached the treatment room. The second stopped Gu halfway across the floor.

He opened the door.

Two travellers stood outside carrying a third man between them. They wore plain road clothes, but both watched the street with the discipline of trained escorts. Blood soaked the blindfold around the injured man's eyes, though the wound beneath it was old. Fresh cuts crossed his ribs. His hands were wrapped around a cracked bronze bell no larger than a fist.

Qin Luo had once been World #6.

Most of Wuyue believed he had vanished into retirement after losing to Liang Yue. Rumours placed him in monasteries, mountain tombs and one northern court that did not exist.

The man at the door did not resemble a rank.

He resembled someone who had remained alive several hours beyond reason.

Rhen reached him before he fell.

Qin's head turned toward the movement. The direction was slightly wrong, as though he followed the pressure of feet through wood but received the answer too late.

[[speaker:qin]]“Physician?”

[[speaker:rhen]]“Yes.”

[[speaker:qin]]“Good.”

His grip loosened from the bell.

[[speaker:qin]]“Do not let them repair my eyes.”

Then he lost consciousness.

Sera's expression changed.

The twelve apprentices had never seen the Pale Orchid take command of a room. One breath she was the woman arguing about water. The next, every doorway, hand and threat had a place.

[[speaker:sera]]“Han, clear the centre table. Gu, lock the rear gate. Bai, descriptions from both carriers before they leave. Lin, check whether we were followed. Nobody says his name outside this room.”

Chen froze at the name.

Seo struck his shoulder hard enough to restart him.

The travellers protested that they could not stay. One had a poisoned cut beneath his sleeve; the other had broken two fingers. Mei read the fear beneath their urgency and let them go only after Rhen closed the poisoned wound and Bai recorded where Qin had been found.

[[speaker:bai]]“Who attacked him?”

[[speaker:customer]]“We did not see. We found him beneath the quarry road. There were no bodies, only marks in the stone.”

[[speaker:lin]]“What kind of marks?”

The traveller looked toward Qin.

[[speaker:customer]]“Circles. Hundreds.”

Sera ended the questions before fear turned them into unreliable witnesses. Gu led the pair through the rear lane separately so nobody outside saw whom they had delivered.

Rhen cut away Qin's blood-soaked robe.

The visible wounds were severe. Three ribs broken. Lung bruised. Poison threaded through the tissue beside the spine. One wrist had been dislocated and reset badly enough to damage the tendons.

The damage beneath them was worse.

Each breath sent a faint vibration through Qin's body and received no answer. The meridians that had once turned sound, stone and rain into a living map had been broken in precise sequence. Not merely blocked. Shattered, scarred, then forced to circulate until the injuries widened.

Seo went pale.

[[speaker:dabin]]“Someone destroyed the pathways deliberately.”

Rhen placed two fingers below Qin's collarbone. A pulse travelled inward so delicately that the apprentices saw nothing. Qin's body reacted anyway. Every muscle tightened against pain too old to be defensive.

[[speaker:rhen]]“Yes.”

[[speaker:sera]]“Can you restore them?”

Rhen did not answer quickly.

That frightened her more than certainty would have.

[[speaker:rhen]]“I can repair the injuries. Whether his cultivation recognizes the repaired structure will depend on Qin.”

[[speaker:sera]]“And the eyes?”

Rhen loosened the bloodied blindfold. Beneath it, the skin held old ritual scars and recent abrasions from rough cloth, but no new injury to the eyes themselves.

[[speaker:rhen]]“Not part of the damage.”

He covered them with clean fabric and began issuing instructions.

Han monitored the organs. Minseok prepared poison-drawing medicine. Tang wrote the sequence of treatments so no exhausted hand would repeat a dose. Yeo stabilized the lower circulation. Everyone else moved outside the quiet boundary Rhen marked around the table.

Sera stood at its edge.

Outside, the dry garden waited for water.

Inside, a bell that could no longer ring lay beside the strongest healer alive.

title: The Bell That Could Not Ring
text:
Qin's treatment lasted through two nights and most of a third day.

Rhen began by doing less than everyone expected.

He stopped the bleeding. Stabilized the organs. Removed fragments of foreign qi buried near the spine. He corrected the wrist and rebuilt the damaged tendons. He did not immediately touch the destroyed vibration meridians.

Chen could not understand why.

[[speaker:chen]]“Every hour creates more scar tissue.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“And every repair changes the structure the next repair depends upon.”

[[speaker:chen]]“But if the pathways close—”

[[speaker:rhen]]“Then we reopen what can bear being reopened. If we restore everything at once, pressure from the first meridian may tear the second before it exists.”

Rhen drew Qin's damaged circulation on six sheets of paper. The pathways looked like a river system after an earthquake: old channels cut apart, false channels forced open, pressure collecting where no healthy body could release it.

Qin's art had once carried vibration through all of them at once.

Now the faintest sound injured him.

Rhen wrapped the treatment room in silence. Rain struck the roof without reaching Qin's bed. Footsteps became pressure without sound. Even breathing seemed to soften.

No technique was announced. The twelve only saw translucent frost gather briefly along the window frame.

The silence created problems of its own. Bai had to stand at the boundary and pass written messages. Han counted Qin's pulse with her fingers instead of a timing bell. Tang created cards for every medicine and turned them face down after each dose so nothing could be repeated by mistake.

Sera remained beside the bed whenever the shop allowed it. She served tea at the front, checked the farm, settled two supplier disputes and returned before every major stage of treatment.

On the second night, Qin woke.

His unseeing eyes stayed closed beneath clean cloth.

[[speaker:qin]]“How many people?”

[[speaker:sera]]“In the room?”

[[speaker:qin]]“Breathing.”

Sera glanced around. Rhen, Han, Yeo, herself.

[[speaker:sera]]“Four.”

Qin's fingers tightened against the blanket.

[[speaker:qin]]“I hear none of you.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“That is intentional.”

Qin turned toward Rhen's voice with an accuracy that came from memory rather than present sensation.

[[speaker:qin]]“My eyes?”

[[speaker:rhen]]“Congenitally blind. Healthy within that truth. Untouched.”

Some tension left Qin's jaw.

[[speaker:sera]]“Why did you warn us?”

[[speaker:qin]]“People hear blind and assume broken. Powerful physicians assume difficult means desirable.”

He drew one slow breath.

[[speaker:qin]]“A royal healer once spent six months promising my clan he could make me normal. I was seven. Every treatment damaged the senses I did possess.”

Rhen adjusted one needle.

[[speaker:rhen]]“I treat injuries. I do not correct identities.”

Qin was quiet for a long time.

[[speaker:qin]]“Then we understand one another.”

He slept again.

Afterward, Han remained beside the table, studying the circulation drawings.

[[speaker:mira]]“If you repair the vibration meridians, will he return to World #6?”

[[speaker:rhen]]“No.”

The answer surprised her.

[[speaker:rhen]]“Healing restores the possibility of work. It does not manufacture the years of practice lost inside an injured body.”

[[speaker:mira]]“Then what are we giving him?”

[[speaker:rhen]]“A road.”

On the third morning, Rhen began the reconstruction.

The apprentices worked in rotations. Han monitored the whole body. Yeo held the lower circulation stable. Seo checked every trace of foreign qi. Minseok prepared medicines to prevent scar contraction. Tang tracked which restored pathway would alter pressure in the next.

Rhen repaired no meridian as a separate line. He rebuilt relationships: where vibration entered, how it dispersed, which tissue carried it safely and where Qin's own qi would need to learn the route again.

The first pathway ran from the right palm through the forearm. Rhen restored less than half, then stopped. Qin's pulse adapted around it.

The second linked the sternum to the inner ear and jaw, allowing vibration carried by bone to become direction. Old scar tissue resisted. Rhen dissolved it grain by grain so the surrounding nerves did not lose the history Qin had built around them.

The third passed downward through the spine.

That was where the foreign qi waited.

It had been shaped to awaken when touched, turning repair pressure back through the injured channels. Seo noticed its rhythm shift before Rhen reached it.

[[speaker:dabin]]“Stop.”

Every hand froze.

She pointed to the smallest change on the circulation sheet.

[[speaker:dabin]]“The residue is answering you.”

Rhen withdrew enough pressure for the trap to settle.

[[speaker:rhen]]“Good.”

Seo did not smile, but her shoulders changed.

They isolated the foreign qi and drew it into a prepared frostroot solution. The liquid blackened, then cracked the bowl.

Hours passed.

At sunset, the cracked bronze bell on the table trembled.

Nobody had touched it.

Qin's hand moved beneath the blanket.

The bell answered with the smallest possible note.

Qin gasped.

Pain crossed his face, followed by something sharper.

Recognition.

[[speaker:qin]]“The table is cedar.”

Han looked at Rhen.

The table was cedar.

Qin's fingers shifted by a breath.

[[speaker:qin]]“Four people. One near the window.”

Yeo was standing near the window.

[[speaker:qin]]“One leg is shorter.”

Sera almost laughed. She had complained about that leg for weeks.

The bell quieted.

Qin's awareness vanished with it, but the pathway had answered once.

Rhen withdrew his hands.

His expression remained calm. Only Sera noticed that the cup of water beside him had frozen solid.

[[speaker:sera]]“Enough?”

[[speaker:rhen]]“For today.”

She guided him outside before any apprentice could ask why the world's strongest healer looked tired.

Rhen sat on the rear step. Sera placed hot tea between his hands, though both knew temperature had nothing to do with what he needed.

[[speaker:sera]]“You told Han healing does not restore cultivation.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“It does not.”

[[speaker:sera]]“But you think he can rebuild it.”

Rhen looked through the open door at Qin's still hand beside the bell.

[[speaker:rhen]]“He already answered once.”

Behind them, Qin slept beside a bell capable of ringing again.

title: What Healing Cannot Manufacture
text:
Qin woke to the vibration of rain.

Not sound.

The roof carried thousands of tiny impacts into the beams. The beams passed them into the walls. The walls returned a dim shape of the room: bed, table, bowl, a person standing perfectly still near the door.

The world did not return whole. It arrived in separate pieces with no agreement about distance. The bowl felt closer than his hand. Rain beneath the eaves seemed to fall inside his chest. One loose floorboard became louder than the entire building.

Qin waited until the pattern settled enough to speak.

[[speaker:qin]]“Rhen.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“Yes.”

[[speaker:qin]]“You do not vibrate properly.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“I have been told I am difficult.”

Qin sat slowly. His restored meridians trembled under the effort. They were healed structures, not recovered mastery. Every pulse brought too much information or none.

Rhen placed the bronze bell in his palm.

[[speaker:rhen]]“Your cultivation must learn the routes again.”

[[speaker:qin]]“How long?”

[[speaker:rhen]]“I do not know.”

Qin accepted the answer more easily than reassurance.

He remained under their roof. At first he crossed rooms with a cane because vibration returned in fragments. The apprentices tried not to hover. They failed.

On the fourth day, Chen moved a stool out of Qin's path.

Qin walked directly into the new position.

[[speaker:qin]]“If you wish to help, stop moving the world.”

Chen never moved his stool again.

Mei announced herself every time she entered until Qin asked whether she believed he had also forgotten her footsteps. Gu walked too quietly, so Qin made him cross the hall twenty times while striking the bell at different strengths. Bai developed a habit of describing everything within reach. Qin finally handed her a cup and asked her to describe only what vibration could not tell him.

[[speaker:bai]]“The glaze is blue.”

[[speaker:qin]]“Useful.”

[[speaker:bai]]“There is a badly painted fish on the side.”

[[speaker:qin]]“Less useful.”

[[speaker:bai]]“Sera likes the fish.”

From the counter, Sera looked up.

[[speaker:sera]]“I tolerate the fish.”

Qin kept the cup.

Recovery became work measured in ordinary distances. Bed to door. Door to stairs. Stairs to courtyard. Qin struck the bell once before each route and tried to hold the returning shape without allowing pain to scatter it.

Rhen never caught him unless he was truly falling.

The first time Qin crossed the courtyard alone, a chicken moved through the path. He stopped before touching it.

Patient Three pecked his cane.

[[speaker:qin]]“What is that?”

[[speaker:rhen]]“A recurring medical concern.”

Sera found Qin in the dry garden one dawn, barefoot on the earth. His bell rested against his sternum. Each controlled hum travelled downward and returned through his feet.

[[speaker:sera]]“You should be resting.”

[[speaker:qin]]“I am.”

[[speaker:sera]]“That is an irritating answer.”

[[speaker:qin]]“Your husband uses it.”

She decided recovery had made him too observant.

Qin tilted his head.

The garden contained vibrations the building concealed: roots moving moisture, insects beneath soil, the shallow catch basin nearly empty. Below all of them ran something steadier.

[[speaker:qin]]“There is water beneath us.”

Sera stopped.

Rhen joined them carrying tea. He did not look surprised, which meant he had hoped Qin would find it and refused to make the attempt into a test.

Qin struck the bell once. The note sank through the courtyard. His face tightened as damaged pathways struggled to interpret the return.

[[speaker:qin]]“A narrow stream. Twelve feet down near the old wall. It divides around stone, rejoins beneath the plum trees, then falls toward the road.”

Rhen unrolled the tile map.

Qin traced the blue string without seeing it.

At the point where Rhen's information had ended, Qin continued. He marked a hollow beyond the rear foundation and a shelf of granite thick enough to carry the kitchen's weight.

[[speaker:qin]]“Cut here. Not closer to the wall.”

The well digger returned that afternoon. He objected to taking directions from a blind patient until Sera asked whether his previous dry shaft qualified him to object.

Following Qin's measurements, he cut a narrow shaft beyond the foundation. The first ten feet produced dust. At eleven, the stone changed colour. Before sunset, clean running water entered the channel without touching the cellar.

The farm survived.

That night, the apprentices celebrated as though Qin had discovered a river. Chen lowered a bucket three times merely to hear it strike water. Tang assigned a schedule before anyone could waste the supply. Minseok carried the first measure to the moon-vine and stopped himself from pouring too much.

Sera found Qin alone at the edge of the courtyard, listening to water move through the new channel.

[[speaker:sera]]“You could stay.”

[[speaker:qin]]“I am still a patient.”

[[speaker:sera]]“That was not a medical statement.”

He understood.

The air around the tea house carried a strange, constant refinement. Qin felt it most clearly when his circulation failed. Something gentle caught the imbalance before it tore, guided excess qi away and left his meridians fractionally denser than before.

Rhen's passive did not replace cultivation. It made every careful repetition matter more.

Qin turned toward the kitchen, where twelve apprentices were arguing about who had overwatered the moon-vine.

Staying meant being known while unfinished. It meant allowing people to move around him without controlling every footstep. It meant owing something that could not be settled through rank or battle.

[[speaker:qin]]“For now.”

Sera nodded as if that were all she had offered.

From the doorway, Rhen watched both of them.

[[speaker:qin]]“And Physician?”

[[speaker:rhen]]“Yes?”

[[speaker:qin]]“Thank you for not giving me sight.”

Rhen's answer came without ceremony.

[[speaker:rhen]]“You never needed it.”

Rain moved through Qin's restored world.

For the first time since his injury, it did not hurt.

title: One More Bowl at Dinner
text:
Making room for Qin required moving three shelves, one treatment cabinet and Rhen's winter-coat chest.

The shelves caused the argument.

[[speaker:sera]]“They cannot go beside the stairs.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“They fit.”

[[speaker:sera]]“People also need to fit.”

Qin stood in the hall while they debated around him.

[[speaker:qin]]“I can sleep in the vibration room.”

There was no vibration room.

Rhen looked thoughtful.

Sera pointed at him.

[[speaker:sera]]“Do not build another room.”

By evening, he had converted the quiet rear chamber into one.

Qin's bell hung from a cedar frame. Different boards covered sections of floor so he could retrain against wood, stone, packed earth and hollow space. Rhen added medical rails along the walls and pretended they were not there to catch him.

The apprentices added a sign reading SECOND SPRING RESONANCE WARD.

Sera replaced it with QIN'S ROOM.

Ren carved a shallow notch beside the doorway, waist-high and impossible to mistake beneath Qin's fingertips. Bai admitted all twelve had argued about its placement. Gu wanted a metal marker that would answer vibration. Mei argued that Qin should be able to find his room without striking the bell and announcing himself to the entire house.

They chose the notch.

Qin touched it once.

He did not thank them aloud.

They understood anyway.

At dinner, thirteen bowls crowded the long table. Sera had extended it with one narrow board supported by medicine crates. Anyone placing an elbow near the join caused three bowls to tilt.

Chen and Seo argued about whether vibration could identify poison inside a sealed jar. Minseok insisted the more important question was why anyone had placed poison near dinner. Bai relayed both arguments to Qin even though he could hear them perfectly well.

Han served rice. Mei removed the chilli from Qin's portion after noticing he disliked the smell. Gu sat nearest the outer door by instinct. Tang positioned the soup where it could not fall across the unstable join.

Qin listened to the household arrange itself around him.

[[speaker:qin]]“Are meals always like this?”

[[speaker:sera]]“No.”

A bowl shattered in the kitchen.

[[speaker:sera]]“Sometimes they are louder.”

Rhen placed soup beside her.

She looked into it.

[[speaker:sera]]“This contains medicinal bark.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“A small amount.”

[[speaker:sera]]“Dinner is not a treatment.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“Everything can be supportive.”

The apprentices had begun watching their exchanges like theatre.

Sera noticed.

[[speaker:sera]]“Eat.”

Thirteen heads lowered immediately.

Conversation resumed in smaller pieces. Jiang asked Qin whether former ranked fighters received pensions. Qin said only if they retired through approved channels, which disappearing while wounded apparently did not satisfy. Lin asked whether the people who injured him would search Lanyun.

The table quieted.

[[speaker:qin]]“If they knew I lived, yes.”

Sera set down her spoon.

[[speaker:sera]]“Then they will not know.”

[[speaker:qin]]“That may bring danger beneath your roof.”

[[speaker:sera]]“Danger has previously found me under less convenient roofs.”

The apprentices heard a joke. Qin heard the absence of one.

Rhen poured more soup.

[[speaker:rhen]]“The roof is already crooked.”

[[speaker:sera]]“The sign is crooked.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“Related condition.”

The argument released the room. Chen began explaining a theory about sealed jars again. Seo told him the theory contained no testable claim. Dinner continued.

Afterward, Qin attempted to help wash bowls. Sera took the first from him, then stopped herself before taking the second.

He washed slowly, locating each edge through touch and the returning tap of ceramic against water. He broke nothing.

Patient Three entered through an unsecured rear door and stole cabbage from the preparation board.

Qin caught the chicken by vibration before Gu found the open latch.

[[speaker:qin]]“Recurring concern.”

Rhen accepted the bird from him.

[[speaker:rhen]]“Improving diagnosis.”

The final cup came later than usual. Sera carried two cups outside, paused at the doorway and returned for a third.

Qin sat beneath the crooked sign with them. He could feel the wood creak in the wind and the faint pulse of the underground stream behind the tea house.

[[speaker:sera]]“This is normally private.”

[[speaker:qin]]“Then why invite me?”

[[speaker:sera]]“Temporary exception.”

Rhen handed Qin a cup.

[[speaker:rhen]]“She likes you.”

[[speaker:sera]]“I permit his continued existence.”

Qin tasted the tea.

[[speaker:qin]]“Warm endorsement.”

Sera looked offended. Rhen looked pleased that someone else had said it.

For several minutes, nothing required them. The apprentices argued behind the shutters about sleeping space. Water moved beneath the farm. Qin rested one hand against the step and learned the quiet shape of the street.

A horse stopped at the edge of the road.

The rider did not enter. He wore the brown sash of the provincial revenue office and kept one hand near the short baton at his waist. He nailed a folded notice to the post beside the tea house and left before Sera reached the road.

She opened it.

PROVINCIAL MEDICINAL CULTIVATION AND CLINICAL LICENSE REVIEW.

All independent growers and healers were required to register their land, stock and patients within ten days. Fees exceeded the farm's entire seasonal income. Failure meant confiscation of unlicensed medicine and closure of treatment rooms.

The notice also demanded patient names, home villages and outstanding payments.

At the bottom sat the seal of Governor Duan Jicheng.

Qin heard the paper tighten in Sera's hand.

[[speaker:qin]]“Bad news?”

[[speaker:sera]]“Expensive news.”

Rhen held out her cup before she could begin planning aloud.

[[speaker:rhen]]“Final cup.”

She looked at him.

[[speaker:rhen]]“Tomorrow.”

For one more minute, they remained beneath the crooked sign as husband, wife and unexpected guest.

Then Sera folded the notice with perfect care.

Year One's peace had received its first invoice.
